title: Filipino-Style Pork Adobo with Eggs & Steamed Rice
dek: Pork belly and shoulder braise in soy, cane vinegar, garlic, bay and cracked pepper until tender, then share their glossy sauce with jammy eggs and hot jasmine rice.
image_alt: Bowl of glossy Filipino-style pork adobo made with browned pork belly pieces and halved braised eggs beside steamed white rice and sliced cucumber
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb boneless pork belly, skin removed and cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
1 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder, trimmed and cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
10 garlic cloves, peeled and lightly crushed
1/2 cup Filipino cane vinegar or unseasoned rice vinegar
1 1/2 cups water, plus more if needed
1 1/2 tsp whole black peppercorns, lightly cracked
2 cups jasmine rice, rinsed until the water runs mostly clear

instructions.name: Dry and season the pork
instructions.text: Pat both cuts of pork very dry and season with the kosher salt. Keep the belly and shoulder in separate piles so the fattier belly can brown first and render enough fat for the leaner shoulder.

instructions.name: Brown in deliberate batches
instructions.text: Heat the neutral oil in a 5- to 6-quart Dutch oven over medium-high. Brown the belly in two batches for 3 to 4 minutes per broad side; transfer to a plate. Spoon off all but 2 tablespoons fat, then brown the shoulder in two batches. Crowding the pot will steam the meat instead of building the browned flavor that anchors the sauce.

instructions.name: Bloom the garlic
instructions.text: Reduce the heat to medium. Add the crushed garlic and cook for 45 to 60 seconds, stirring, until fragrant and pale gold. Do not let it turn dark or it may become bitter during the braise.

instructions.name: Start the adobo braise
instructions.text: Return all pork and accumulated juices to the pot. Add the vinegar, soy sauce, 1 1/2 cups water, bay leaves, peppercorns and brown sugar if using. Bring to a boil without stirring for 2 minutes so the vinegar's raw edge cooks off, then stir once, cover and reduce to a low simmer.

instructions.name: Cook the eggs and rice
instructions.text: While the pork braises, lower the eggs into simmering water and cook for 9 minutes. Chill in ice water for 5 minutes and peel. For the rice, combine the rinsed rice and 2 1/2 cups water, bring to a boil, cover, reduce to low and cook for 15 minutes; remove from the heat and rest covered for 10 minutes before fluffing.

instructions.name: Braise until spoon-tender
instructions.text: Simmer the pork covered for 45 minutes, then turn the pieces and continue for 15 to 25 minutes. Pork is safe at 145°F followed by a 3-minute rest, but shoulder and belly become properly tender closer to 195°F to 205°F; a fork should twist into the largest shoulder piece with little resistance. Add 1/4 cup water if the liquid falls below one-third of the meat.

instructions.name: Season the eggs in the sauce
instructions.text: Add the peeled eggs to the pot for the final 10 minutes of covered cooking, turning once so they color evenly. Transfer the pork and eggs to a platter and discard the bay leaves.

instructions.name: Reduce to a glossy finish
instructions.text: Bring the sauce to a lively simmer and reduce uncovered for 6 to 10 minutes, skimming excess fat, until it lightly coats a spoon. Return the pork and eggs, turn to glaze, and taste before adding salt because soy sauces vary. Halve the eggs and serve with rice, cucumber and scallions.

why_it_works: Combining meaty shoulder with rich belly gives the sauce body without making every bite overwhelmingly fatty.
Boiling the vinegar briefly before stirring softens its sharp raw aroma while preserving the bright acidity that keeps the pork from tasting heavy.
Reducing the braising liquid only after the tender pork is removed prevents the meat from breaking apart while the sauce concentrates.
swaps: Use 3 pounds pork shoulder for a leaner adobo; add 1 tablespoon neutral oil when browning and expect the sauce to have slightly less body.
Chicken thighs can replace the pork. Brown them skin-side down, then braise until they reach at least 165°F, usually 30 to 35 minutes, before reducing the sauce separately.
For gluten-free adobo, use certified gluten-free tamari. Apple-cider vinegar works in place of cane vinegar but tastes fruitier, so omit the optional sugar at first.
storage: Cool the pork, sauce and eggs promptly and refrigerate in a shallow airtight container for up to 4 days; refrigerate the rice separately for up to 4 days. Reheat the adobo gently on the stovetop with 2 to 3 tablespoons water until the pork and sauce reach 165°F. Reheat rice covered with a spoonful of water until steaming throughout. Freeze the pork and sauce without eggs for up to 3 months.
notes: A low-sodium soy sauce leaves room to reduce the sauce without making it aggressively salty. Taste only after reduction.
The cucumber is more than garnish: its cool crunch balances the rich pork and salty-tangy glaze seen in the finished dish.
Adobo is especially good made one day ahead. Chill it, lift off the firm surface fat, then reheat gently and add freshly cooked rice.

faqs.q: Why did my adobo sauce turn too salty?
faqs.a: The soy sauce may have been full-sodium or the liquid reduced too far. Add hot water 2 tablespoons at a time, then balance with a small splash of vinegar. Next time, use low-sodium soy and stop reducing when the sauce just coats a spoon.

faqs.q: Can I stir the vinegar as soon as it goes into the pot?
faqs.a: The dish will still work, but letting the vinegar boil undisturbed for about 2 minutes is a useful traditional technique that cooks away its harshest raw aroma before the sauce is mixed.

faqs.q: How do I keep the eggs from becoming rubbery?
faqs.a: Cook them separately for 9 minutes, chill immediately, and add them only for the last 10 minutes of the braise. They absorb color and flavor without spending an hour at simmering temperature.

title: Crispy Herb Falafel with Pita & Lemon-Tahini Sauce
dek: Soaked chickpeas, parsley, cilantro, cumin and coriander fry into deeply crisp falafel with fluffy green centers, ready for warm pita and a silky lemon-tahini dip.
image_alt: Five deep-golden oval falafel on a brown platter beside torn warm pita, leafy greens and a small bowl of pale lemon-tahini sauce
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups dried chickpeas (about 10 oz), sorted and rinsed
1 packed cup flat-leaf parsley leaves and tender stems
1 packed cup cilantro leaves and tender stems
1 small yellow onion, roughly chopped (about 1 cup)
2 tbsp chickpea flour, plus 1 tbsp if needed
6 cups neutral high-heat oil, for frying
1/3 cup cold water, plus more as needed
1/2 tsp kosher salt, for the sauce
4 pocket pitas, warmed and torn or halved
2 cups chopped romaine or tender salad greens

instructions.name: Soak dried chickpeas overnight
instructions.text: Place the chickpeas and 1/2 teaspoon baking soda in a large bowl and cover with at least 4 inches of cool water. Soak for 12 hours at room temperature; the chickpeas should more than double in size but remain raw. Drain, rinse and spread on a clean towel to dry thoroughly.

instructions.name: Pulse a coarse, cohesive mixture
instructions.text: In a food processor, pulse the dried soaked chickpeas, parsley, cilantro, onion, 5 garlic cloves, cumin, coriander, 1 1/4 teaspoons salt, black pepper and cayenne in 1-second bursts. Scrape the bowl repeatedly and stop when the mixture resembles coarse couscous and holds when squeezed; do not purée it into hummus.

instructions.name: Rest and test the falafel base
instructions.text: Transfer to a bowl and mix in baking powder, 2 tablespoons chickpea flour and sesame seeds. Cover and refrigerate for 20 minutes. Shape one tablespoon into a firm oval; if it cracks apart, mix in the remaining tablespoon chickpea flour rather than adding water.

instructions.name: Whisk the lemon-tahini sauce
instructions.text: Whisk the tahini, lemon juice, grated garlic and 1/2 teaspoon salt. The mixture will seize; whisk in the cold water a tablespoon at a time until pale, smooth and pourable. Add another tablespoon or two of water if needed, then refrigerate until serving.

instructions.name: Shape compact ovals
instructions.text: Scoop packed 2-tablespoon portions and shape into 16 compact balls or ovals about 1 1/2 inches wide. Set on a parchment-lined tray. Press firmly enough to remove cracks, but do not compress them into dense pucks.

instructions.name: Heat the oil accurately
instructions.text: Pour oil into a heavy, deep pot to a depth of about 2 inches, leaving at least 3 inches of headroom. Heat over medium to 350°F. Keep a lid nearby, never leave the oil unattended, and do not add wet food to hot oil.

instructions.name: Fry in small batches
instructions.text: Lower 4 falafel into the 350°F oil with a spider or slotted spoon. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden and crisp; keep the oil between 335°F and 355°F. Drain on a wire rack over a sheet pan, return the oil to 350°F, and repeat. The centers should be steaming and about 190°F.

instructions.name: Build the pita plate
instructions.text: Warm the pitas in a dry skillet or a 325°F oven until flexible. Arrange the crisp falafel with pita, greens, cucumber and tomato, and serve the lemon-tahini sauce alongside. Serve immediately while the crust is at its best.

why_it_works: Dried soaked chickpeas retain enough structure to fry crisp and fluffy; canned chickpeas contain too much cooked moisture and often produce soft, fragile falafel.
Short pulses create tiny distinct chickpea pieces that lock together while leaving steam pathways for a light center.
A measured 350°F oil temperature sets the outside quickly without burning it before the raw chickpea center cooks through.
swaps: Use all parsley or all cilantro if that is what you have, but keep the total packed herb volume at 2 cups for a fresh, green center.
For gluten-free falafel, confirm the baking powder and chickpea flour are certified gluten-free and serve with gluten-free flatbread or a chopped salad.
To avoid deep frying, brush shaped falafel generously with oil and air-fry at 375°F for 12 to 15 minutes, turning halfway. The crust will be lighter and less even than the photographed fried version.
storage: Refrigerate cooked falafel in a shallow airtight container for up to 4 days and the sauce separately for up to 5 days. Reheat falafel on a rack in a 400°F oven or 375°F air fryer until crisp and 165°F inside, about 6 to 10 minutes. Freeze cooled falafel in a single layer, then bag for up to 3 months; reheat from frozen at 375°F for 12 to 15 minutes.
notes: The 810-minute total includes a 12-hour soak and a 20-minute refrigerator rest; active work is about 45 minutes.
Do not use canned chickpeas for this fried method. They are already cooked and hold substantially more water, which changes both texture and frying behavior.
If the first test falafel breaks in the oil, mix 1 more tablespoon chickpea flour into the remaining batch and let it rest for 5 minutes before trying again.

faqs.q: Why did my falafel fall apart in the oil?
faqs.a: The chickpeas may have been wet, the mixture too coarse, or the oil below temperature. Dry the soaked chickpeas thoroughly, pulse until a squeezed portion holds, add the reserved chickpea flour if needed, and fry one test piece at 350°F.

faqs.q: Can I prepare the mixture a day ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Process the chickpea-herb mixture without baking powder, cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Mix in the baking powder, flour and sesame shortly before shaping and frying.

faqs.q: How can I tell when falafel is cooked inside?
faqs.a: A finished falafel should be deeply brown outside, steaming and evenly green-beige inside rather than wet or pasty. A probe inserted through the side should read about 190°F; maintain the oil near 350°F so the center and crust finish together.

title: Bakery-Style Cinnamon Rolls with Vanilla Cream Cheese Frosting
dek: A tangzhong-enriched dough bakes into tall, pillowy cinnamon spirals under a generous blanket of tangy vanilla cream cheese frosting.
image_alt: Rectangular metal pan filled edge to edge with tall golden cinnamon rolls covered generously in white vanilla cream cheese frosting
ingredients: 1/4 cup bread flour (30 g), for the tangzhong
1/2 cup whole milk (120 g), for the tangzhong
3/4 cup whole milk (180 g), warmed to 100°F to 105°F
3 3/4 cups bread flour (450 g), plus up to 2 tbsp if needed
6 tbsp unsalted butter (85 g), very soft
6 tbsp unsalted butter (85 g), softened, for the filling
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar (150 g)
1 tbsp bread flour (8 g), for the filling
1/4 tsp kosher salt, for the filling
4 oz full-fat cream cheese (113 g), softened
1 tbsp whole milk, plus more if needed
1/8 tsp kosher salt, for the frosting

instructions.name: Cook the tangzhong
instructions.text: Whisk 1/4 cup bread flour and 1/2 cup milk in a small saucepan over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the whisk leaves clear lines and the paste reaches about 150°F. Scrape into the mixer bowl and cool for 10 minutes, until warm rather than hot.

instructions.name: Mix a soft enriched dough
instructions.text: Add the warm milk, yeast, granulated sugar, eggs, 1 teaspoon salt and 3 3/4 cups bread flour to the tangzhong. Mix with the dough hook on low for 3 minutes until no dry flour remains, then rest the shaggy dough for 10 minutes so the flour hydrates.

instructions.name: Knead in the butter
instructions.text: Knead on medium-low while adding the 6 tablespoons soft butter one tablespoon at a time. Continue for 8 to 10 minutes until the dough is glossy, elastic and clears most of the bowl while remaining slightly tacky. Add extra flour only 1 tablespoon at a time if it still smears like batter after 8 minutes.

instructions.name: Complete the first rise
instructions.text: Transfer the dough to a lightly greased bowl, cover and let rise in a draft-free 75°F to 80°F spot for 60 to 75 minutes, until visibly puffy and about doubled. A cooler kitchen may require another 20 to 30 minutes; judge the dough, not only the clock.

instructions.name: Make the cinnamon filling
instructions.text: Mix the brown sugar, cinnamon, 1 tablespoon bread flour and 1/4 teaspoon salt. The small amount of flour absorbs melting butter so more filling stays in the spirals instead of pooling under the rolls.

instructions.name: Roll, fill and cut evenly
instructions.text: Roll the dough on a lightly floured surface into an 18-by-14-inch rectangle, with a long side facing you. Spread with the 6 tablespoons filling butter, leaving a 1/2-inch bare strip along the far edge, and sprinkle evenly with cinnamon sugar. Roll up snugly from the near long side, pinch the seam, and cut into 12 equal rolls with unflavored dental floss or a serrated knife.

instructions.name: Proof in the pan
instructions.text: Arrange the rolls cut-side up in a buttered 9-by-13-inch metal pan. Cover and rise for 35 to 50 minutes, until the rolls look marshmallow-soft, touch one another and spring back slowly when gently pressed. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 350°F with a rack in the center.

instructions.name: Bake to a tender center
instructions.text: Bake at 350°F for 23 to 28 minutes, rotating the pan once, until the tops are golden and the center roll reaches 190°F to 195°F. If the tops brown before the centers are ready, tent loosely with foil. Cool in the pan for 15 minutes before frosting.

instructions.name: Frost generously while warm
instructions.text: Beat the cream cheese and 4 tablespoons butter until completely smooth. Beat in confectioners' sugar, vanilla, 1 tablespoon milk and 1/8 teaspoon salt until fluffy; add another teaspoon milk only if needed. Spread over the warm, not piping-hot, rolls so the frosting softens into the spirals without melting away.

why_it_works: Tangzhong pre-gelatinizes a portion of the flour's starch, allowing the dough to hold extra milk while staying manageable and tender for longer.
Adding butter after the flour hydrates lets gluten develop before fat coats the proteins, producing tall rolls with a shreddable crumb.
A temperature check at the center roll prevents the common tradeoff between raw middles and overbaked edges.
swaps: All-purpose flour can replace bread flour by weight. Hold back 2 tablespoons of the main-dough milk at first, then add it only if the dough feels firm because all-purpose flour absorbs slightly less liquid.
For orange cinnamon rolls, add 1 tablespoon finely grated orange zest to the filling and replace the frosting milk with fresh orange juice.
To prepare overnight, shape the rolls, cover the pan tightly and refrigerate for up to 14 hours. Let stand at room temperature for 60 to 90 minutes until puffy before baking.
storage: Because of the cream cheese frosting, refrigerate covered rolls within 2 hours and keep for up to 4 days. Reheat one roll loosely covered in the microwave for 15 to 25 seconds, or warm several covered at 300°F for 10 to 12 minutes. Freeze unfrosted baked rolls for up to 2 months; thaw, warm and frost before serving.
notes: The 220-minute total includes both rises, the 10-minute dough rest and 15 minutes of cooling before frosting; active work is about 45 minutes.
A metal 9-by-13-inch pan browns the bottom and sides more predictably than glass. If using glass, begin checking 5 minutes early because heat retention differs.
Measure the flour by weight if possible. Scooped cups can vary enough to turn a soft bakery-style dough into dry bread.

faqs.q: Why did my cinnamon rolls turn out dense?
faqs.a: The dough may have received too much flour, insufficient kneading or an incomplete rise. Keep it slightly tacky, knead until elastic, and let each rise continue until the visual cues are met even if your kitchen is cool.

faqs.q: Can I make these without a stand mixer?
faqs.a: Yes. Stir with a sturdy spoon, then knead by hand for 12 to 15 minutes, working the soft butter in gradually. Use a bench scraper instead of adding large amounts of flour when the dough sticks.

faqs.q: How do I keep the filling from leaking into the pan?
faqs.a: Use very soft rather than melted butter, include the tablespoon of flour in the cinnamon sugar, leave a clean edge for sealing, and proof in a properly sized pan so the rolls support one another.
